title: Examples UIs
narrative:
This is an overview of the various example UIs
    in the test suite.

    This specification also ensures that the
    various UI examples in the test suite,
    run successfully and also produce
    UIs with expected state and appearance.

features.id: The advanced UI define in the examples has the expected state.

extraInfo: The advanced UI example is absolutely packed with things to see. Yet, at the same time, it is not too much code and also not too complicated. It really shows you how boilerplate code can be reduced to a minimum when using SwingTree.

features.id: The login example UI defined in the examples, a good MVVM demonstration.

extraInfo: The login example view, together with the login example view model, is a really basic example of how to do MVVM with SwingTree. For a more advanced example, see the user registration example.

features.id: The user registration example UI defined in the examples, a good MVVM demonstration.

extraInfo: The user registration example, together with the user registration example view model, is a more advanced example of how to do the MVVM design pattern with SwingTree. It involves a lot of input validation that is done in the view model. For a more basic example, see the login example view.

features.id: The list examples UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: The list search example view, together with the list search example view model, is a small MVVM example demonstrating how to populate a list of items and filter them through a search field — both driven by observable properties on the view model.

features.id: The box shadow picker example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: Not only is the box shadow picker example an advanced example of how to write MVVM applications with SwingTree, it is also a nice little tool that shows you how to use the SwingTree style API to override the default look and feel of Swing components.

features.id: The MVI based box shadow picker example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: Not only is the box shadow picker example an advanced example of how to write MVI applications with SwingTree, it is also a nice little tool that shows you how to use the SwingTree style API to override the default look and feel of Swing components.

features.id: The glass view example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: The glass view example is an advanced styling example which demonstrates how you can apply a glass effect to components using a custom filter configuration. As you can see, the component centered in the middle of the view has a glass effect, which consists of a blur as well as a scaling on the background provided by the parent. Under the hood, this works by rendering the parent into a buffered image and then when a child component is rendered, it uses the parent's buffered image for the filter effect.

features.id: The breathing helper example can be instantiated correctly.

extraInfo: The breathing companion view, together with the breathing view model, is a calming demo whose whole reason for existing is to show off SwingTree animations inside a clean Model-View-Lenses (MVL) architecture. A glowing orb swells as you breathe in, rests, shrinks as you breathe out, and rests again — every frame derived from the immutable view model. Run the view class directly to see the animation in action.

features.id: The neumorphic step sequencer example can be instantiated correctly.

extraInfo: PULSE, the neumorphic step sequencer, together with its immutable view model, is a little drum machine whose entire visual identity is carved out of light and shadow (the "soft UI" / Neumorphism style): every pad is the same slate colour as its surface and inverts from raised to pressed-in when toggled, using SwingTree's named-shadow API. It is also a tour of three SwingTree ideas at once: pure-data MVI with a Tuple<Track> and per-track ValueSet<Integer> patterns, the modelled re-armed animation pattern driving a tempo-accurate playhead, and reactive styling combined with custom painter(..) based rotary knobs. Run the view class directly to play with it.

features.id: The animation example view can be created.

extraInfo: The animated view example demonstrates several different animation techniques in one place — looping, transitional and event-driven animations all driven via the animateFor(..) API. Run the class directly to see them in action.

features.id: The transitional style animation example view can be created.

extraInfo: The transitional style animation example shows how a single boolean property can drive a smooth two-state transition using the withTransitionalStyle(..) API. See the matching "An Advanced Style Animation" wiki guide for a walk-through of how the mechanism works.

features.id: The SVG viewer example view can be created.

extraInfo: The SVG viewer example demonstrates how to load and render vector graphics inside a SwingTree UI — useful for icons and other resolution-independent artwork.

features.id: The markdown text viewer example view can be created.

extraInfo: The markdown text viewer example shows how SwingTree can render rich text content together with a custom markdown parser into a regular Swing component.

features.id: The spinners example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: The "some components" example view bundles spinners, sliders and other small input components into a single view that is bound to the matching view model. It's a handy reference for property bindings on input widgets that aren't text fields.

features.id: The list rendering example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: The list rendering example demonstrates how to declare a JList with a custom cell renderer using SwingTree's fluent withCell(..) / cell-builder API — the same approach shown in the "Writing Tables" wiki guide, applied to lists.

features.id: The `NamedFieldsView` example UI defined in the examples can be created.

extraInfo: The named fields example is a tiny example of how to attach a textual name(..) label to a form field so the resulting UI is both accessible and visually consistent across a settings panel.

features.id: The `ListTestExample` class can be created.

extraInfo: The list test example is a sandbox for SwingTree's various list-like factories. Useful when you want to compare how scrollPanels, list and other list-style builders behave side by side.

features.id: The `TeamView` class can be created.

extraInfo: The team view example is the self-contained showcase for the MVI / MVL "addAll over a tuple lens" pattern walked through in the "Functional MVVM" wiki guide. Each team member is rendered through a sub-view bound to its own lens property focused on a tuple item.

features.id: The MVVM twin of the `TeamView` class can be created.

extraInfo: The MVVM team view example renders the very same UI as the MVI team view example, but wires it up in the classical MVVM way: mutable Var / Vars properties on the view model instead of lenses into one immutable record. The two exist side by side so the difference between the patterns is the only thing that differs.

features.id: The `CalculatorView` class can be created.

extraInfo: The MVI calculator example is the runnable companion to the calculator walk-through in the "Functional MVVM" wiki guide — three immutable records and one runCalculation() wither produce the entire UI behavior.

features.id: How SwingTree code compares to a GUI Editor based implementation.

extraInfo: This example GUI serves as a comparison between SwingTree and an identically looking implementation based on NetBeans's GUI Editor. This class is an implementation that is editor based, whereas this class uses SwingTree to achieve the same appearance. Here we only check that it is rendered as expected, but the really interesting part is how the two implementations compare to each other side by side. As you can see, the components of this view each have unique layout requirements which can be difficult to handle. The SwingTree implementation demonstrates nicely how the requirements can be met without much boilerplate using the various MigLayout keywords and layout modes. Feel free to visit the two examples and run them yourself, they each have main methods for that purpose already.

features.id: The todo app UI defined in the examples has the expected state.

extraInfo: The todo app example is a small, self-contained example of building a vertically stacked list of task panels — useful as a starting point for any "list of editable items" UI.

features.id: The scroll pane UI defined in the examples can be instantiated without errors.

extraInfo: The scroll-pane configuration example demonstrates the various scroll-pane construction options exposed by SwingTree — including the fluent scrollPane(it -> ...) configurator and the scrollPanels() factory that lets you stack many child panels inside a single scrolling container.

features.id: The basic hover example UI defined in the examples can be instantiated without errors.

extraInfo: The hover example demonstrates how onMouseEnter / onMouseExit can drive style or content changes — the simplest possible building block for hover interactions in SwingTree.

features.id: The basic border hover example UI defined in the examples can be instantiated without errors.

extraInfo: The border hover example demonstrates the same hover trick as the basic hover example, but applied to the component's border — a nice way to highlight interactive elements without disturbing their layout.

features.id: The `FoldableExample` can be created.

extraInfo: Check out the foldable panel example if you want to see an example of how to create a panel with a folding animation based on the withTransitionalAnimation(Var, ...) method.

features.id: The tab selection binding examples, all start off with the third tab selected.

extraInfo: The tab selection example demonstrates how to bind the currently selected tab of a JTabbedPane to a property on the view model. Each instance of the example is instantiated with a fresh view model whose initial state selects the third tab — so all three instances we create below should report selectedIndex == 2.

features.id: The tasks manager examples can be created error free.

extraInfo: We instantiate both the classical MVVM tasks view (built on mutable properties) and the functional MVI / MVL tasks view (built on an immutable record-based view model) side by side. Comparing the two implementations is a good way to see how the same UI shape can be expressed in either architecture.

features.id: The chat UI examples can be created error free.

extraInfo: We instantiate both the classical MVVM chat view and the functional MVI / MVL chat view side by side. The MVI variant is the one walked through in the "Functional MVVM → Dealing with Lists" wiki guide and demonstrates addAll(Var<Tuple<…>>, ...) on a tuple lens — the recommended pattern for dynamic lists of sub-views.
